title: Why Success Still Feels Empty | Jane Marie Chen, Founder of Embrace
guest: Jane Marie Chen, founder and former CEO of Embrace (low-cost infant incubators), author of the memoir Like a Wave We Break, now a leadership coach
summary: A director's cut replay of the hosts' conversation with Embrace founder Jane Marie Chen about childhood abuse, achievement as a trauma response, burnout after shutting down her company, and the multi-year healing journey she chronicles in her memoir. Jane shares tools such as The Body Keeps the Score, internal family systems 'parts work', inner-child conversations, the 'whole body yes' test, boundaries with family, and surrendering outcomes. The hosts reflect on slowing down, untangling achievement from identity, and asking where your drive to achieve comes from.

ideas.idea: For many high achievers with perfect-looking resumes, achievement is a coping mechanism and a trauma response to feeling 'not enough'.
ideas.detail: Jane says people with perfect outsides often come from histories of trauma; they feel they must do more, be more and prove more, and burn out in the process. She sees this especially in entrepreneurs and social entrepreneurs.

ideas.idea: Feeling powerless as a child became the fuel to help the most powerless people in the world, but that same drive had a shadow side that pushed her to unhealthy work levels.
ideas.detail: Jane's team invented a low-cost incubator for premature babies at Stanford in 2008; she moved to India, set a goal of saving one million babies, and 'gave her soul' to it for ten years until a setback forced the company to shut down and she felt like a complete failure. Her line: 'my pain became my purpose.'

ideas.idea: Children of immigrants over-achieve because of cultural expectations, the pressure to justify their parents' sacrifice, and a sense that nothing is ever good enough.
ideas.detail: Jane says no number of degrees, accolades or babies saved could fill the void, which she traces to childhood abuse: a child wonders 'what's wrong with me' and the adult tries to prove they are worthy. The hosts add the feeling of carrying the weight of all your ancestors and 'living out their dreams'.

ideas.idea: Pressure to succeed creates healthy drive until it tips into 'needing to prove', so develop awareness of what your motivations really are.
ideas.detail: Jane says wanting to do good for healthy reasons and needing to prove yourself coexisted in her; the hosts extend this: if your drive comes from a place you are comfortable with, use it as courage, but if it is to prove something to the exterior world it is the darker side of the shadow.

ideas.idea: Achievement becomes safety and belonging for kids who grew up as outsiders.
ideas.detail: Jane moved to the US at four without a word of English, in one of the only Asian families in her neighborhood, with parents who did not speak English; achieving gave her a sense of belonging.

ideas.idea: Cycles of abuse get normalized in Asian culture as a cultural norm, so calling them out publicly helps others feel seen and less alone.
ideas.detail: Jane did not recognize her childhood beatings as abuse until her late 30s; the suicide of a Taiwanese-American high school friend from a violent home made her realize her silence was complicity. The hosts note that 'saving face' in Asian culture makes her candor especially brave.

ideas.idea: Trauma is not left in the past; it rewires the brain and nervous system and is stored in the body and limbic system, so you cannot talk your way out of it, you have to feel your way through.
ideas.detail: Reading The Body Keeps the Score by Bessel van der Kolk was a turning point. Talk therapy never worked for Jane because trauma lives in the emotional limbic system, not the thinking neocortex; she later 'stalked' van der Kolk until he became her therapist.

ideas.idea: You cannot CEO your way through healing: instead of spreadsheeting modalities and pivoting fast, you have to slow down and feel the heartbreak, fear and anger you ran from.
ideas.detail: Jane bought a one-way ticket to Indonesia with a surfboard and attacked healing with founder intensity, keeping a spreadsheet of modalities and hunting for a 'magic elixir'. Healing only began when she slowed down with teachers, healers and friends who created a safe space. Cherie relates as a 'doer and fixer' who A/B tests solutions.

ideas.idea: Internal family systems 'parts work' treats your overachiever, perfectionist and inner-critic parts as protectors of younger parts carrying shame, and asks for compassion toward each rather than banishing them.
ideas.detail: Jane realized her save-the-world part was protecting a very young part that never felt enough; an ex nicknamed her warrior part 'Genghis Khan'. She recommends the book No Bad Parts and offers a free parts-work exercise on her website.

ideas.idea: Everything you seek externally you have to find internally, because when you rely on external validation the goalposts keep moving.
ideas.detail: At a van der Kolk psychodrama retreat Jane recruited a Santa-Claus-looking man and later a friend to play her 'ideal father' reading scripted lines, and felt nothing. She only felt something when she read the lines ('you're enough, you're worthy') to a photo of herself at age five that sits on her desk.

ideas.idea: Have compassion for your parents' whole story and lineage while still holding boundaries; understanding does not condone abuse but it brings inner peace.
ideas.detail: Writing the book meant exploring how her parents grew up and how trauma seeps into family systems. Her practice is to be open-hearted and boundaried simultaneously, tuning into her body's contraction around toxic behaviors and then choosing not to be around them. Holding resentment hurts yourself; her greatest freedom was feeling it and letting it go.

ideas.idea: Confronting your parents is not about changing them; it is about taking the hand of your inner child and standing up for her, so you can trust yourself.
ideas.detail: Leadership coach Diana Chapman of the Conscious Leadership Group pushed Jane to talk to her parents, which she called the scariest thing she has ever done. She went in without expecting change, since expecting others to behave a certain way creates suffering; the hosts note saying your piece is itself the therapy whether or not the other person absorbs it.

ideas.idea: The more you say no to certain things, the stronger your yeses become, and healthy family boundaries let you engage more wholeheartedly without underlying resentment.
ideas.detail: Jane says boundaries with family are hard because we want to love them, especially around holidays, but boundaries remove the angst that poisons the relationship.

ideas.idea: Use the 'whole body yes' test: only commit when head, heart and gut align; anything that produces contraction deserves a pause and the question 'do I really want this, to what end?'.
ideas.detail: A whole-body yes feels to Jane like an effervescent line of energy lifting up her body. On book tour she was offered three events in one New York day; old Jane would have done all three and been wiped, but she did one. The hosts joke that for overachievers the achievement is to not overachieve.

ideas.idea: If you drive too hard in unhealthy ways you burn bright and then burn out completely; sustainable impact requires daily self-care.
ideas.detail: After shutting down Embrace, Jane had a complete mental and physical breakdown that took about a year and a half to recover from, discovering her mind could be that fragile after believing she was invincible. Cherie connects this to 'what got you here won't get you there': the next level requires letting go rather than white-knuckle grinding.

ideas.idea: Control is an illusion; give something your all and then surrender the outcome, because the magic happens when you let go.
ideas.detail: For ten years Jane tried to control everything at Embrace and met setback after setback; the minute she let go, Tony Robbins came in out of nowhere and saved the company. Before her book launch, overwhelmed by pressure to make it a bestseller, she held a ceremony in Honolulu throwing her only copy into the ocean (then burning and burying it under a tree). Jean adds that over-optimizing leaves no room for serendipity beyond your imagination.

ideas.idea: Redefine success as living your values every day (love, giving, growing) rather than external outcomes, because 'success without fulfillment is the ultimate failure'.
ideas.detail: Jane quotes Tony Robbins and notes many outwardly successful people are empty inside, always comparing to the next person while the goalpost moves; values are the part you can control.

ideas.idea: Self-compassion is the rubber coating on the glass ball of your identity: untangle achievement from who you are so one failed speech or unpopular post cannot shatter you.
ideas.detail: Jean offers the glass-ball image; Jane endorses it, saying we are worth more than the sum of our achievements or our social media likes, and worries about a younger generation whose sense of self collapses when a post underperforms.

ideas.idea: To start feeling again after years of numbness, sit in stillness and notice small physical sensations, since every emotion has a bodily correlate, and heal in community rather than isolation.
ideas.detail: Jane's memoir line is 'we cannot heal what we cannot feel'; at first she felt nothing, but patience brought sensations. Friends, therapists and teachers create the safety that lets the nervous system relax enough to access emotion.

ideas.idea: Weave a daily or weekly practice of slowing down and introspection into your life, because constant grinding can be a way to avoid your own thoughts and eventually forces a reckoning.
ideas.detail: Cherie admits being a go-go-go person for whom sitting on a beach with no distractions is scary; she takes from Jane that ignoring it too long leads to the kind of breakdown Jane suffered. The hosts suggest meditation, journaling, and talking to a trusted person or therapist, and ask listeners what their own healing journey would look like.

ideas.idea: Reaching the goal (one million babies saved) matters less than learning that it does not define all of who you are.
ideas.detail: Jane stepped down from Embrace in May after the million-baby goal was reached this year; she says what she is proudest of is learning to 'embrace myself', and now teaches leadership coaching at corporate and individual levels via janemariechen.com.
